messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 26
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Editor
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 56

The incident happened eight months ago, on a Thursday evening. He was driving home from the office, a light rain blurring the windshield. He had just finished editing a chapter of a debut novel—a quiet domestic story about reconciliation—and his mind was still half on a character’s arc. A police cruiser behind him, lights flashing. He pulled over immediately, hands at ten and two. He remembers thinking, *I didn’t run a light. I signaled the turn.*

The officer took his license, registration, insurance. Asked if he’d been drinking. He hadn’t. Then a second officer appeared, flashlight in hand, shining it directly into his face. He remembers the white blindness and the smell of rain on asphalt. The second officer asked why he looked so nervous. He said it was his first time being pulled over. A long pause. Then the officer said, “Get out of the car.”

He does not remember the exact sequence of the next few minutes. He knows he was told to spread his legs, hands on the trunk. He knows the officer’s forearm pressed into his back, a knee against his thigh. He knows he heard the word “resist” shouted, though he had not moved. And he knows that when he finally sat back in his car, hands shaking, the officers were standing by their cruiser laughing. He was given a verbal warning for a broken taillight. The broken taillight did not exist.

Now, in the present, he is an editor, but the work feels different. He sits at his desk with a client’s manuscript—a memoir about a cross-country road trip—and he cannot get past page two. Every mention of a highway shoulder, a gas station at night, the shriek of a police siren in a distant sentence—he has to stop. He rereads the same paragraph four times. His chest tightens. He gets up and walks to the window and checks the street for blue and red lights. There are none. He knows this. He sits back down.

His wife, a social worker, has tried to help. She suggests they take walks together after dinner, but he avoids the main road. He suggests they drive instead, but then he drives only on residential streets, deliberately slow, checking the rearview mirror every few seconds. Once, they were stopped at a light and an unmarked sedan pulled up beside them. He thought he saw a badge on the belt of the driver. His hands began to tremble. He was certain he heard a voice say, *“Get out of the car.”* His wife put her hand on his arm and asked what was wrong. He said nothing, but the sweat on his forehead would not dry.

He has stopped meeting friends for coffee downtown. Too many patrol cars. He has started working from home three days a week, even though his boss prefers in-person collaboration. He tells himself it saves commute time, but the truth is he cannot stand the thought of being pulled over again. The memory is not a single scene. It is a loop of fragments—the flashlight, the forearm in his back, the laughter. He has not told his wife about the nightmares. She wakes to find him sitting upright, hands gripping the sheet, breathing fast. He says it was a dream about falling. She does not push.

When he opens his email, he sees a draft of an author’s note that reads, *“I would like to thank the police officers who showed me compassion during a difficult time.”* He closes the email. He does not edit it. He saves it for another day.

His posture has changed. He walks with his shoulders slightly hunched, as if bracing for a command. At night, in bed, he listens to the quiet hum of the furnace, the distant wail of a siren growing louder and then fading, and he tells himself the sound is everywhere, it is normal, it means nothing. But his jaw tightens. His eyes stay open long after his wife’s breathing deepens. He waits. And he does not know what he is waiting for, only that the waiting has become his constant silence.
